levels.title: US History: The Big Picture
levels.objective: After this level you can sketch the American story from the first peoples to 2000 through its biggest turning points.

levels.title: The First Americans
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how people first reached the Americas from Asia during the last Ice Age, and why the timing is still debated.

levels.title: A Continent of Nations
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the variety of Native nations, languages and ways of life in North America before 1492.

levels.title: Cahokia, City of Mounds
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Cahokia, the Mississippian city near today's St. Louis, and what its great mounds were for.

levels.title: Towns in the Cliffs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Ancestral Puebloans built the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde.

levels.title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Law of Peace joined five nations into one league, and why its influence on the US Constitution is debated.

levels.title: The Columbian Exchange
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how crops, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic after 1492, and why epidemics devastated Native peoples.

levels.title: Spain Comes North
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Spain founded St. Augustine and New Mexico, and why the Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out in 1680.

levels.title: Jamestown and the Powhatan
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Jamestown survived after 1607, how tobacco made it pay, and how it collided with the Powhatan chiefdom.

levels.title: Checkpoint: First Peoples, New Worlds
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what North America was like before 1600 and how the arrival of Europeans changed it.

levels.title: The Pilgrims and the Wampanoag
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Wampanoag allied with Plymouth, and how the harvest feast of 1621 differs from the later Thanksgiving story.

levels.title: A City Upon a Hill
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Puritans hoped to build in Massachusetts and why they banished dissenters like Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson.

levels.title: Thirteen Colonies, Three Regions
levels.objective: After this level you can compare New England, the Middle Colonies and the Southern Colonies by who settled them and how they made a living.

levels.title: How Slavery Took Root
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how colonial laws turned slavery into a lifelong, inherited status based on race.

levels.title: The Middle Passage
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Atlantic crossing enslaved Africans were forced to endure, and how many were carried to the Americas.

levels.title: King Philip's War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Metacom led New England's Native nations into war in 1675 and what the war cost both sides.

levels.title: Women in the Colonies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain coverture and the work colonial women did, from running households to growing indigo like Eliza Lucas Pinckney.

levels.title: Colonists Govern Themselves
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how elected assemblies and town meetings gave colonists a habit of governing themselves.

levels.title: The French and Indian War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the war of 1754 to 1763 made Britain master of eastern North America but left it deep in debt.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Thirteen Colonies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the thirteen colonies grew, who did their work, and why they were used to running their own affairs by 1763.

levels.title: The Stamp Act Crisis
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Stamp Act of 1765 set off the cry "no taxation without representation", and what Parliament argued back.

levels.title: From Massacre to Tea Party
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts pushed Britain and the colonies toward war.

levels.title: Lexington and Concord
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the shooting war began in April 1775 and why the militia were ready for it.

levels.title: Common Sense
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet turned many colonists from protest toward independence.

levels.title: The Declaration of Independence
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Declaration's argument about rights and consent, and the contradiction with slavery that critics pointed out at the time.

levels.title: How the Colonies Won
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Saratoga, the French alliance and Yorktown let an outmatched army win independence.

levels.title: Loyalists and Native Nations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why many colonists stayed loyal to Britain and why most Native nations sided with the Crown.

levels.title: Liberty and Slavery in the War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how enslaved people sought freedom on both sides of the war, and why northern states began to end slavery.

levels.title: Women and the Revolution
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the parts women played, from boycotts and camp work to Abigail Adams asking her husband to "remember the ladies".

levels.title: Checkpoint: The American Revolution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a tax dispute became a war for independence, and who gained and lost by it.

levels.title: Why the Articles Failed
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Articles of Confederation left the new nation weak, and why Shays' Rebellion alarmed its leaders.

levels.title: The Summer of 1787
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Compromise settled the fight between large and small states at the Constitutional Convention.

levels.title: Slavery in the Constitution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the three-fifths, slave trade and fugitive clauses, and how later Americans argued over what they meant.

levels.title: The Fight Over Ratification
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the Federalists' and Anti-Federalists' arguments, and explain how their fight produced the Bill of Rights.

levels.title: Washington Sets the Pattern
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the precedents Washington set as the first president, from the cabinet to stepping down after two terms.

levels.title: Hamilton, Jefferson and Parties
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Hamilton and Jefferson clashed over a national bank and the country's future, and how the first parties grew from it.

levels.title: The Election of 1800
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the first handover of power between rival parties, after a deadlocked election, mattered so much.

levels.title: The Louisiana Purchase
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the 1803 purchase doubled the country, and what Lewis, Clark and Sacagawea found in lands that were already home to many nations.

levels.title: The War of 1812
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the US fought Britain again in 1812 and how the war ended Tecumseh's hope of a Native confederacy.

levels.title: Checkpoint: A New Republic
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Americans wrote a constitution, argued over it, and made it work in the republic's first decades.

levels.title: The Trail of Tears
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and how the Cherokee won in court but still lost their homeland.

levels.title: Mills, Canals and Newcomers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how factories, canals and Irish and German immigrants transformed the North before 1860.

levels.title: King Cotton
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the cotton gin and the domestic slave trade spread slavery across the Deep South.

levels.title: Life Under Slavery
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the work, family life, faith and culture that enslaved people built under slavery.

levels.title: Resisting Slavery
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the ways enslaved people resisted, from slowing work and escaping to Nat Turner's revolt and the Underground Railroad.

levels.title: The Abolitionists
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Frederick Douglass, William Lloyd Garrison and others argued to end slavery, and why many Northerners opposed them.

levels.title: Seneca Falls, 1848
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Declaration of Sentiments demanded and how the women's rights movement grew alongside abolition.

levels.title: Manifest Destiny
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Texas, Oregon and the Mexican War added the West, and what that meant for the Mexicans and Native peoples already living there.

levels.title: Compromises That Failed
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas-Nebraska Act each tried to settle slavery in the West.

levels.title: Milestone: Colonies to a House Divided
levels.objective: After this level you can connect colonial slavery, the founders' compromises and westward expansion to explain why the nation split by 1860.

levels.title: Dred Scott to Secession
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Dred Scott decision, John Brown's raid and Lincoln's election led Southern states to secede.

levels.title: Fort Sumter and the Border States
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the war began in 1861 and why the border states mattered so much to both sides.

levels.title: The Emancipation Proclamation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the 1863 Proclamation did and did not do, and why Lincoln issued it as a war measure.

levels.title: Black Soldiers, Self-Emancipation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Black soldiers and enslaved people escaping to Union lines helped turn the war into a war against slavery.

levels.title: Gettysburg
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Battle of Gettysburg was a turning point and what Lincoln's address there said the war was for.

levels.title: Total War and the Home Fronts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Sherman's march, the draft and women's war work brought the war to civilians in North and South.

levels.title: Appomattox and Assassination
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how the war ended in April 1865 and what Lincoln's assassination changed.

levels.title: Three Amendments
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments promised and why they are called the second founding.

levels.title: Reconstruction Rises and Falls
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Reconstruction achieved, the violence that opposed it, and the bargain of 1877 that ended it.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Civil War and Reconstruction
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the war ended slavery and what Reconstruction promised, won and lost.

levels.title: Rails, Homesteads and Bison
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the transcontinental railroad and the Homestead Act opened the Plains, and how the bison were nearly wiped out.

levels.title: Wars for the West
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the wars between the US Army and the Plains nations, from Little Bighorn in 1876 to Wounded Knee in 1890.

levels.title: Boarding Schools and Allotment
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how boarding schools and the Dawes Act aimed to erase Native cultures and cost Native nations most of their remaining land.

levels.title: Gilded Age Giants
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Carnegie and Rockefeller built giant companies, and why Americans called such men both robber barons and captains of industry.

levels.title: Workers Organize
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why industrial workers struck and formed unions, and what the Triangle fire of 1911 changed.

levels.title: Ellis Island and Angel Island
levels.objective: After this level you can explain who the new immigrants of 1880 to 1920 were, and how the Chinese Exclusion Act shut out one group.

levels.title: Jim Crow
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how segregation laws, Plessy v. Ferguson and voting barriers undid Reconstruction's gains, and how Ida B. Wells fought back.

levels.title: The Progressives
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how muckrakers and reformers took on monopolies, unsafe food and corrupt city machines.

levels.title: Votes for Women
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how suffragists won the vote state by state in the West and then nationally with the 19th Amendment in 1920.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Rails, Factories, Newcomers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how industry, immigration and the conquest of the West remade the country between 1865 and 1920.

levels.title: 1898 and an Overseas Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the war with Spain in 1898 gave the US overseas colonies, and what imperialists and anti-imperialists argued.

levels.title: World War I
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the US stayed out of World War I until 1917, what each side of the argument over joining said, and what American troops changed.

levels.title: The Great Migration and Harlem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why millions of Black Southerners moved north and how the Harlem Renaissance grew from it.

levels.title: The Roaring Twenties and Prohibition
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what changed in the 1920s, and why Americans banned alcohol in 1920 and repealed the ban in 1933.

levels.title: The Crash and the Dust Bowl
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how ordinary Americans lived through the Great Depression and why the Dust Bowl drove families off the Plains.

levels.title: The New Deal
levels.objective: After this level you can name the New Deal's main programs, including Social Security in 1935, and explain who they helped and who they left out.

levels.title: The Road to Pearl Harbor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the US moved from neutrality to aiding Britain, and why Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941.

levels.title: World War II
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the US fought and won World War II in Europe and the Pacific, from D-Day to Japan's surrender.

levels.title: The Home Front and Incarceration
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how World War II changed work for women and Black Americans, and why Japanese Americans were forced into camps.

levels.title: Checkpoint: World Power, Boom and Bust
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how war, boom and depression between 1898 and 1945 made the US a world power with a bigger federal government.

levels.title: The Cold War Begins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain containment, the Korean War, the nuclear arms race and the Red Scare at home.

levels.title: The GI Bill and the Suburbs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the GI Bill, federal mortgages and interstate highways built the postwar suburbs, and who was shut out.

levels.title: Brown v. Board and Little Rock
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the NAACP's legal campaign won Brown in 1954, and why integrating schools like Little Rock's was still so hard.

levels.title: Sit-ins, Freedom Rides, Marches
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how nonviolent direct action, from lunch counters to the March on Washington, pushed the nation to act.

levels.title: The Space Race and the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Soviet Sputnik launch of 1957 set off a space race and how Apollo 11 reached the Moon in 1969.

levels.title: Vietnam and a Divided Nation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the US fought in Vietnam and why the war divided Americans at home.

levels.title: The Rights Revolution Spreads
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how women, farmworkers and Native activists built on the civil rights movement, from Title IX to tribal self-government, and why the ERA stalled.

levels.title: Immigration Remade
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the quotas of 1924 closed the door to most newcomers and how the Immigration Act of 1965 reopened it.

levels.title: Watergate
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Watergate scandal led to Nixon's resignation in 1974 and what it changed about how presidents are watched.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Superpower and Civil Rights
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Cold War and the civil rights movement reshaped American life and rights between 1945 and 1975.

levels.title: Facts and Interpretations
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a historical fact from an interpretation, using historians' rival explanations of why the colonists rebelled.

levels.title: Reading a Primary Source
levels.objective: After this level you can question a primary source by asking who made it, when, for whom and why, using Frederick Douglass's Fourth of July speech of 1852.

levels.title: What Caused the Civil War?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the evidence on the war's causes, starting with what the seceding states said in their own declarations.

levels.title: Reconstruction Remembered
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how historians' verdict on Reconstruction changed from the Dunning School to W. E. B. Du Bois and later scholars.

levels.title: Did the New Deal Work?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the case that the New Deal rescued the country against the cases that it fell short or went too far.

levels.title: The Decision to Drop the Bomb
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments historians make about why the US used atomic bombs on Japan in 1945.

levels.title: Why the Cold War Ended
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the explanations for the Cold War's end in 1989 to 1991, from American pressure under Reagan to Gorbachev's reforms and the Soviet economy.

levels.title: September 11, 2001
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the attacks of September 11, 2001, and explain why historians treat very recent events differently from the distant past.

levels.title: Myths About American History
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk popular myths, like Washington's cherry tree, and explain how such myths get started and why they last.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: US History
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of US History Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
